evals.prompt: Our TypeScript backend has UserManager, UserService, UserHelper and UserValidator classes, plus an IUserRepository interface with a single UserRepositoryImpl. OrderService.calculateTotal(order) loops over order.getLines(). Redesign this so it's cleaner.
evals.expected_output: Starts from the messages and invariants, moves total calculation to the order (Information Expert) or a pure function beside the Order type, collapses Manager/Helper/Service layers into functions or deletes them, removes the single-implementation interface unless it is a real I/O boundary that needs a fake, wires dependencies in a composition root, and reports in the Design/Objects/Rejected output format.
expectations: Moves the total calculation next to the order data (order.total() or a pure function over the Order type) and names Information Expert or feature envy as the reason
Recommends merging or deleting the Manager/Helper/Service classes rather than adding new layers
Treats IUserRepository as justified only if it is an I/O boundary that needs a fake, otherwise removes it
Does not introduce a DI container, base class, or new interface with a single implementation
Output lists each remaining class with the invariant, role, or resource it owns

evals.prompt: We have class Notification with subclasses EmailNotification, SmsNotification, and now product wants urgent and digest versions of each (UrgentEmailNotification, DigestSmsNotification...). Should I keep adding subclasses?
evals.expected_output: Identifies combinatorial subclass explosion from two independent axes of variation (channel and delivery policy), recommends composition: a channel role and a delivery/formatting role injected into one Notification sender, with channel as an interface because providers are an I/O boundary, and shows a short sketch.
expectations: Names the problem as two independently varying aspects causing subclass explosion
Recommends composition (inject channel and policy roles) instead of more subclasses
Keeps inheritance depth at most one or removes the hierarchy
Includes a code sketch in which a new combination needs no new class

evals.prompt: Our Kotlin pricing code has a sealed interface Product with 4 variants and a when() in each of price(), tax(), shippingWeight() and render(). A reviewer says 'replace conditionals with polymorphism' and wants a class per product type with those four methods. We add new operations roughly monthly and a new product type about once a year. Who's right?
evals.expected_output: Applies the expression-problem rule: operations change faster than types and the variant set is closed and owned, so the sealed interface with exhaustive when is the better design; polymorphism would force touching every class for each new operation. Mentions the Martin-Muratori axis and that the compiler checks exhaustiveness.
expectations: Recommends keeping the sealed interface with exhaustive when expressions
Justifies it by operations changing faster than types (expression problem)
Notes that Kotlin's when over a sealed type is checked for exhaustiveness
States when polymorphism would become the better choice (open set of variants added by others, stable operations)

evals.prompt: Should our orders module and billing module be separate microservices that talk over events?
evals.expected_output: Near-miss: this is a service/module boundary question, not object design. Points to software-architecture (and possibly system-design) rather than producing class diagrams or GRASP analysis.
expectations: Identifies the question as architecture or service boundaries and routes to software-architecture
Does not answer with class-level design, GRASP, or inheritance advice as the main content
